theQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.question: A lease must stop TWO heavy scans on ONE shared database. What is the identity of 'one shared database', given that the fleet names databases by env-var (FACTORY_DATABASE_URL, PRODUCTION_NEONDB_URL, ATOMS_DATABASE_URL, STAGING_NEONDB_URL, ...) and that two env-vars can point at one Postgres instance?
theQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.whyItIsNotObvious: the cheap answer is a declared alias -- 'factory', 'cortex' -- as the lease key, because that is what the dispatch's own prose uses ('the store', 'PARENT_STORE'). It is wrong in a way that will not be noticed until it has already failed: cloudbuild.publish.yaml states, at source, that 'NEONDB and HAUSKA_MCP are the same Neon project (cortex-prod) and the same production/parent branch -- confirmed live 2026-09-07'. Two env-vars, one instance. A caller that declares 'cortex' for one and 'hauska_mcp' for the other takes two leases on one Postgres and both heavy scans run. Worse, a lane could hold an alias lease and a DIFFERENT env-var for the same database would not see it. That is a guard that does not fire, which is the defect class DEV_PROCESS is built around.
theQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.answer: the lease is keyed on the DATABASE HOST -- what src/db/connect.mjs's hostFingerprint() already means (it returns url.hostname) and what runs.db_host_fingerprint already records on every run row. The declared alias is carried beside it as store_alias, for a reader, never as the contention key. Contention is therefore on the Postgres instance (CPU, IO, connections, autovacuum), which is the resource AGENT-CONTRACT section 4 serializes -- not on a logical database name. The consequence is deliberate and one-directional: two logical names for one host contend (correct, and the case the fleet has), and two hosts never contend (falsifier 3).

theOtherQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.question: Extend the existing `leases` table, or a new table?
theOtherQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.whyItIsNotObvious: `leases` already exists (migrations/0001_init.sql) and src/control/leases.mjs already implements take/lock/release with a heartbeat, an expiry, a stolen_from column, and a partial-conflict upsert. Reusing it looks like the cheap, precedent-following answer, and the dispatch explicitly asks for the decision in CP1.
theOtherQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.readAt: src/control/leases.mjs, migrations/0001_init.sql:216-228, and every caller: src/jobs/restamp-access.mjs, src/jobs/p2-juris.mjs, src/jobs/f10-cad-loop.mjs, src/jobs/conformant.mjs.
theOtherQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.answer: a NEW table, heavy_scan_leases, for four measured reasons, in order of weight.
reasons: The identity is a different shape and cannot be expressed. `leases` has PRIMARY KEY (entity_type, county_fips) and CONSTRAINT leases_no_global CHECK (entity_type <> 'GLOBAL' AND county_fips <> 'GLOBAL'). A heavy-scan lease is per DATABASE with an OPTIONAL county -- it has no entity_type at all, and the county is null for a whole-store window. To make it fit, the no-GLOBAL check has to be relaxed, and the table's own guard is the thing that currently stops a caller taking a global writer scope. Weakening the guard on the writer-scope table to hold an unrelated kind of lease is the wrong direction of change.

Contention semantics differ, and the difference is not cosmetic. takeScopedLease's ON CONFLICT ... WHERE leases.expires <= now() makes a scoped writer lease STEALABLE the instant it expires -- correct for a writer scope, where the whole point is that the next writer must get in. A heavy-scan lease must NOT be stolen at expiry by a racer silently: the crash case (falsifier 2) requires the expired lease to be RECORDED as expired, with who reaped it and why, because 'a crashed holder's lease expires; the reaper records it' is a named requirement. Two different release disciplines cannot share one column set without one of them becoming a lie.

The write-frequency profile is opposite. A writer scope is taken once per bulk write and released; a heavy-scan lease is HEARTBEAT-REFRESHED every TTL/3 by a timer for hours. Putting a 3-minute heartbeat update on the same table that answers 'who holds the atoms writer scope for 48021' means every heavy scan anywhere in the fleet makes that reader scan a table with a row churning every few minutes.

P-284 already set this precedent on this exact program and it is recorded: extending `runs` with cost columns was rejected for grain, and the reason was written down. Copying the acceptance criteria rather than re-litigating them is the point of a program contract.
theOtherQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign.whatIsReusedInsteadOfDuplicated: the release vocabulary and the run/termination conventions: refuse-with-a-code (never a bare throw), a named constant per refusal, run_events for the announce/confirm pair, and the existing hostFingerprint(). takeScopedLease itself is NOT touched and is NOT called -- a heavy scan of a database is not a write scope on it, and conflating them would let a heavy scan be blocked by an unrelated county's writer lease.

theSchema.migration: migrations/0013_heavy_scan_leases.sql (NOT applied to any store by this lane)

table_1_heavy_scan_leases.columns: id uuid pk; store text (the contention key: the database HOST fingerprint); store_alias text (what the caller calls it -- factory | cortex | atoms | staging:neondb | production:neondb, for a reader only); store_database text (the URL pathname, e.g. neondb, so an alias can be resolved back to a real target); window_kind ('heavy-scan' | 'job-execution'); holder_kind ('job-execution' | 'session-seat'); holder text (the Cloud Run execution name, or the session seat id); holder_token uuid; phase text (the job id / phase the window is for); county_fips text NULL; run_id uuid NULL REFERENCES runs(id); started_at; heartbeat; expires; released_at NULL; release_kind NULL ('released' | 'expired' | 'reaped'); released_by; reap_reason.
table_1_heavy_scan_leases.theRaceControlIsTheDatabase: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX heavy_scan_leases_one_live_per_store ON heavy_scan_leases (store) WHERE released_at IS NULL. Exactly one live lease per store -- enforced by Postgres, not by a read-then-write in the application. Two racing takers cannot both succeed: the loser receives a unique violation, which the helper translates to LEASE_HELD after re-reading the row so the refusal can NAME the holder it lost to (falsifier 1, dispatch item 4). This is the same lesson P-284 recorded in its own words: 'the three-state rule has to be a CHECK in the schema, not a convention in the writer -- the writer is the thing that would be wrong.'
table_1_heavy_scan_leases.constraints: window_kind IN ('heavy-scan','job-execution'); holder_kind IN ('job-execution','session-seat'); store <> ''; holder <> ''; county_fips IS NULL OR ~ '^[0-9]{5}$'; expires > started_at; (released_at IS NULL AND release_kind IS NULL) OR (released_at IS NOT NULL AND release_kind IN ('released','expired','reaped')); released_at IS NULL OR released_at >= started_at; UNIQUE (holder_token).
table_1_heavy_scan_leases.why_city_not_required: a heavy scan of the factory store by the publish job is county-scoped; the hourly gate scheduler is not. A lease that forced a county would force a caller that does not have one to invent one, and an invented county is a guess stored as fact.

table_2_heavy_scan_lease_refusals.columns: id; refused_at; store; store_alias; window_kind; holder (who was refused); holder_kind; phase; county_fips; lost_to_lease_id uuid NULL REFERENCES heavy_scan_leases(id); lost_to_holder text NOT NULL; lost_to_window_kind; lost_to_expires; reason_code (LEASE_HELD).
table_2_heavy_scan_lease_refusals.whyASeparateTable: dispatch item 4 -- 'every refusal is written with the holder it lost to.' A refusal is not a lease: it has no holder_token, no expiry and no release, and putting it in the lease table would mean either a row that is never live or a nullable explosion. It is also the only durable evidence that the control FIRED -- a control observed only passing is a control nobody has seen work (DEV_PROCESS; lane-claim.mjs's own self-test header says the same thing).
table_2_heavy_scan_lease_refusals.whyLostToHolderIsDenormalisedAsText: lost_to_lease_id can go stale (the lease is swept and, in a future compaction, deleted). The holder NAME cannot. The refusal must still read correctly in a year, which is the whole reason it is written.

theSchema.view_heavy_scan_lease_live: one row per live lease (released_at IS NULL AND expires > now()), naming store, alias, window_kind, holder, holder_kind, phase, county_fips, taken_at, heartbeat, expires, seconds_remaining. Live means BOTH unreleased and unexpired -- a lease past its expiry is not live even though it still blocks a taker until it is swept, and those two facts must not be shown as one.

theRunnerHelper.exports: HEAVY_LEASE_REFUSED_CODES; DEFAULT_TTL_MS (30 min); renewalIntervalMs(ttl); storeFingerprintFromUrl/fromEnv; takeHeavyScanLease(client, spec); renewHeavyScanLease(client, spec); releaseHeavyScanLease(client, spec); reapExpiredHeavyScanLeases(client, {now, reapedBy}) -> the rows it expired; listHeavyScanLeases(client, {store}); withHeavyScanLease(client, spec, fn, {onEvent}) -> { result, lease }.
theRunnerHelper.take_semantics: one transaction: (1) SELECT the unreleased rows for this store FOR UPDATE; (2) any row whose expires > now() is a live holder -> write a heavy_scan_lease_refusals row naming its holder and raise LEASE_HELD; (3) any row whose expires <= now() is swept in place (released_at=now(), release_kind='expired', released_by=<taker>, reap_reason='expired unreleased') -- this IS the reaper recording a crashed holder, and it is why falsifier 2 says 'proceeds after expiry, not before'; (4) INSERT the new lease. A unique violation at step 4 (a racer won between 1 and 4) is re-read and reported as LEASE_HELD with the winner named, never as a generic failure.
theRunnerHelper.renew_semantics: UPDATE ... SET heartbeat=now(), expires=now()+ttl WHERE holder_token=$1 AND released_at IS NULL RETURNING expires. Zero rows is LEASE_LOST and is LOUD: the holder's window is gone and it must stop, because somebody may now be scanning the same store.
theRunnerHelper.release_semantics: UPDATE ... SET released_at=now(), release_kind='released', released_by=<holder> WHERE holder_token=$1 AND released_at IS NULL. Idempotent: a second release is a no-op, not an error, so a finally that runs twice is harmless.
theRunnerHelper.withHeavyScanLease_semantics: take -> write the ANNOUNCE event (run_events kind 'heavy-lease-taken', body = store, alias, window_kind, holder, expires, expected duration) -> start an UNREF'd interval renewing every ttl/3 -> await fn(lease) -> in a finally: stop the timer, release, write the CONFIRM event (kind 'heavy-lease-released', body = held_ms, renewals, lost, result_counts). AGENT-CONTRACT section 4 requires announce-then-confirm and this is where it is discharged. The interval is unref'd on purpose: a renewal timer must never be the reason a Cloud Run job's event loop stays alive.
theRunnerHelper.the_lost_lease_is_checkable: lease.assertHeld() does a fresh renew and throws LEASE_LOST if it fails. The two wired cell jobs call it at every city boundary and the publish bake calls it at every page boundary -- so a holder that lost its window stops at the next boundary instead of running to completion while another holder scans. Falsifier 2's 'not before' half depends on this being a real check and not a comment.
theRunnerHelper.no_compute_or_geometry_is_touched: the helper reads and writes four tables (heavy_scan_leases, heavy_scan_lease_refusals, run_events, and runs only by reference) and executes no PostGIS.

job_side: src/jobs/parcel-setback-cells.mjs -- runParcelSetbackCells takes the lease on the CORTEX host (the store its CITY_ALL_PARCELS_SQL full scan runs against) around the city loop, wraps the existing startRun/writeTermination block, and calls assertHeld() per city. The window kind is 'heavy-scan'.

src/jobs/parcel-envelope-cells.mjs -- the same shape. Its heavy statement is PARCEL_AREA_SQL (ST_MakeValid/ST_Union/ST_Area over txgio_parcel), which is the heaviest single statement in the fleet, and it runs against the same cortex host, so the two jobs contend with each other exactly as section 4 requires.

src/jobs/bastrop-publish.mjs -- the bake step (runChunkedConformantBakes) is a full-county multi-hour bake, so it takes a 'job-execution' window on the TARGET store's host (resolved from the target's own env var, never a hardcoded name) for the duration of the chunk loop, with assertHeld() per page. It is taken AFTER requirePreBakeReadiness and the coverage floor, so a refusal by those gates never holds a lease.

src/jobs/reap.mjs -- the existing tick (verb 'reap') additionally calls reapExpiredHeavyScanLeases for every store, so an abandoned lease is recorded on a schedule and not only when the next taker arrives.

session_side.script: scripts/heavy-scan-lease.mjs on THIS LANE'S doc_repo SEAT BRANCH (lane/p281-heavy-leases), never on P:/doc_repo main. Verbs: list | take | release | renew | check.
session_side.transport: the factory-control API. src/control/api.mjs gains GET /heavy-scan-leases, POST /heavy-scan-lease-take, POST /heavy-scan-lease-release, POST /heavy-scan-lease-renew, behind the createControlServer bearer auth that already guards every route. The dispatch offered 'through the factory-control API or a read-only check plus a documented take call'; the API is chosen because it is the only path that works from a session with no database credential, and because the alternative (a documented-but-unbuilt take call) is a control that cannot fire.
session_side.credential: FACTORY_CONTROL_API_URL (the service URL) plus FACTORY_CONTROL_API_KEY (the bearer token, mounted as a Cloud Run secret on the console-audit job; see cloudbuild.console-audit.yaml's --set-env-vars for the URL form). The VALUE IS NEVER PRINTED by the script, and the script's refusal output names the variable, never the value. No database credential is needed and none is read, which is the point: a session can take a heavy-scan lease without holding FACTORY_DATABASE_URL.
session_side.the_honest_failure_mode: the endpoints exist in this lane but are NOT deployed (this lane does not deploy). Until the integration seat ships the revision, the script gets 404 and refuses with ENDPOINT_NOT_DEPLOYED, naming the revision that must ship. It does NOT fall back to a local file or to a silent no-op -- a lease that only exists in the caller's imagination is exactly the 'guardrail that does not survive a clone' DEV_PROCESS refuses.
session_side.what_a_session_lease_means: holder_kind 'session-seat', holder = the seat id from _catalog/seat_register.json, window_kind 'heavy-scan', county optional. It exists so an interactive session about to run a heavy scan by hand announces itself to the fleet the same way a job does.

theWiring.self_grant_analogy: NOT applicable and deliberately so: AGENT_CONTRACT's self-grant ruling is about the deploy-traffic lease in _catalog/leases/, which is a coordination file, not a control. A heavy-scan lease is a mutual-exclusion control and there is nothing to 'self-grant' -- the database already decides.

preRegisteredFalsifiers.note: Quoted from the dispatch before any code was written. The predictions below are the answers this lane commits to in advance; the rig is named so a stranger can re-run it.

F1.claim: Two runners racing for the same store: exactly one proceeds; the other exits non-zero with the holder named.
F1.predicted: two REAL node processes, launched within the same 100 ms against one scratch Postgres and one store fingerprint. Exactly one prints TAKEN and the other exits non-zero with code LEASE_HELD and a message naming the winner. The decision is made by the partial unique index, so the loser's failure is a Postgres unique violation translated into LEASE_HELD -- not an application-level if. The loser also leaves a heavy_scan_lease_refusals row whose lost_to_holder names the winner.
F1.wouldFalsify: both processes obtaining a lease (an app-level read-then-write that raced), or a loser that exits 0, or a refusal that does not name who beat it.

F2.claim: A holder killed mid-run: its lease expires and the next runner proceeds after expiry, not before.
F2.predicted: process A takes a lease with a short TTL (a --ttl-seconds override exists for exactly this) and is killed with taskkill /F -- no release, no finally. Process B, started before A's expiry, is REFUSED with LEASE_HELD and A named. Process B, started after A's expiry, PROCEEDS and A's row is left with release_kind='expired', released_by=B, reap_reason='expired unreleased' -- the reap is recorded on the row, not inferred from the absence of a release.
F2.wouldFalsify: B proceeding before expiry, or B proceeding after expiry by DELETING/ignoring A's row (a reap nobody can read), or A's row surviving as unreleased with B's lease alongside it (two live rows on one store).

F3.claim: Different stores do not block each other.
F3.predicted: two leases on two different host fingerprints are both taken, both listed live, and neither refusal table gains a row. This is the negative direction of F1 and is asserted in the same test file, because a control observed only blocking has not been observed working.
F3.wouldFalsify: any second-store take refused, or a list output that shows one store when two are held.

F4.claim: Named bypass: a job or script that never calls the helper. List every heavy job that does not yet.
F4.predicted: the list is produced by MEASURING src/ (which files execute a PostGIS aggregation or an unindexed full-table scan against a shared store) and is returned with each entry's evidence, split into 'wired by this lane' (3 jobs + the reaper sweep), 'heavy and NOT wired, with the row that owns it', and 'examined and NOT heavy, with the reason'. An empty bypass list is not a predicted outcome and would itself be the finding.
F4.wouldFalsify: a bypass list produced by listing job files rather than by reading their SQL, or a 'not heavy' entry with no statement quoted.

designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.extend_the_existing_leases_table: REJECTED -- see theOtherQuestionThatDecidedTheDesign. Four reasons, the first two decisive: the (entity_type, county_fips) primary key plus the no-GLOBAL CHECK cannot express 'per database, county optional' without weakening the guard that currently stops a caller taking a global writer scope; and the existing ON CONFLICT ... WHERE expires <= now() STEALS an expired scope silently, which is right for a writer and wrong for a rare exclusive window whose crash case must be RECORDED.
designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.key_on_a_declared_store_alias: REJECTED on the measured fact that two env-vars in this fleet point at one Neon project and branch (cloudbuild.publish.yaml, confirmed live 2026-09-07). An alias-keyed lease would let one Postgres instance carry two live heavy scans, which is the only thing the control exists to prevent.
designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.key_on_the_full_connection_string: REJECTED as a leak and a false negative at once: it carries the password, and two URLs differing only in query parameters would be two 'stores'. The host is what hostFingerprint() already means and what runs.db_host_fingerprint already stores.
designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.a_file_in_doc_repo_like_the_traffic_leas: REJECTED, and the dispatch names why: 'Cloud Run jobs cannot read doc_repo files', and the existing hook only arms inside doc_repo-rooted sessions. A control that is invisible to exactly the processes that do the heavy scanning is not a control.
designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.a session-only advisory lock (pg_advisor: REJECTED: an advisory lock is scoped to a SESSION, so it cannot outlive the process that holds it, cannot be seen by a cell in a console, and vanishes with the connection. This control must survive a kill -9 and be readable afterwards.
designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.make_the_lease_a_rail_or_a_gate_verdict: REJECTED. A rail verdict is a statement about a county's data, computed on a schedule, and the gate has no production caller for anything but the publish refusal. A lease is a statement about a running process. Writing one into the other is how a `verdict` column starts meaning two things -- which is the P-201 finding this program is still paying for.
designAlternativesConsideredAndRejected.auto_expiring_without_a_reap_record: REJECTED. If a taker could take an expired lease by simply inserting over it, the crashed holder would vanish with no record, and 'why did two heavy scans overlap on 2026-09-17' would be unanswerable. The expired row is CLOSED with a reason and a reaper before the new one is opened.

howThisControlCouldBeWrongAndStillLookRi: It serializes nothing because every caller names a different store. The alias is NOT the key, and the key is derived from the connection the caller is already using, so the only way to get a different key is to genuinely be on a different host. The residual risk is a caller passing a HAND-BUILT store string instead of one derived from its own connection; the take API requires store to be supplied explicitly (so tests can use fake stores), so this is real. Closed as far as it can be: storeFingerprintFromEnv/fromUrl are the exported ways to get one, the take signature records store_alias and store_database beside it so a mismatch between the declared alias and the actual connection is visible in the row, and F3 asserts two hosts do not contend rather than asserting anything about aliases.

It blocks a heavy scan against a lease held by a process that is already dead but not yet reaped. That is BY DESIGN for the window before expiry (fail closed, not open), and the remedy is the expiry plus the reaper tick. Stated so it is not mistaken for a defect: this control prefers a false refusal to a missed collision, and the refusal NAMES the holder, which is what makes the false refusal cheap to resolve by hand.

It lets the publish job's 'job-execution' window (hours) starve a session's 'heavy-scan' (minutes) for the whole bake. Judged correct -- the bake is the thing that must not be disturbed -- and made visible by list showing window_kind, holder and expires so a session can see how long it must wait instead of guessing. If practice shows this is too coarse, window_kind is already in the row and can be added to the contention key without a data migration; it is NOT in the key now because two live windows on one database is precisely what section 4 forbids.

A renew timer that silently stops makes the lease expire under a running job. Closed by making renew's zero-row result a LOUD lease-lost and by assertHeld() at every city/page boundary, so the job stops at a boundary. The failure mode left open: a single SQL statement that runs longer than the TTL with no boundary to check at. TTL is 30 minutes and the longest single statement in these jobs is a per-county aggregation; if a statement ever exceeds the TTL the row expires and a second scanner may start, and the record will show it because the first holder's renewals stopped.

The refusal record itself becomes the thing that fails. A take that cannot write its refusal because the store is unreachable will surface a connection error rather than LEASE_HELD. Accepted and stated: the control's failure to RECORD is reported as its own error and never as a successful take.
adversarialReviewOfMyOwnPlan.howThisCouldBeOverBroad: A heavy-scan lease taken around a WHOLE JOB rather than around the heavy statement would serialize short jobs against long ones for no reason and train people to work around the control. The wired jobs take it around their actual scan/work loop only, and the two cell jobs take it on the CORTEX host they scan, not on the factory store they write -- because the scan is the contended resource. The cost of that choice: a factory-store heavy scan run by a job that never touches cortex is not covered by these three wirings, which is why the bypass list (F4) is a required deliverable and not an appendix.

scopeBasis: hauska-factory (the branch is cut from PR #158's head, see whereThisLaneBuildsFromAndWhy) plus one script and this lane's artifacts in its own doc_repo seat worktree. Inside hauska-factory the footprint is: migrations/0013_heavy_scan_leases.sql (new), src/control/heavy-lease.mjs (new), src/control/api.mjs (four routes added, no existing route changed), src/jobs/reap.mjs (one call added to the existing tick), the three jobs the dispatch names, src/cli.mjs (a heavy-lease verb group, for the integration seat and for the reaper's own manual sweep), and tests. Stated exclusions so a successor can tell a decision from an oversight: (a) NO migration is applied, nothing is deployed, no Cloud Run job is executed, no production or staging store is read or written -- the only database this lane touches is a scratch PostgreSQL container it starts and disposes of, and the two contention falsifiers are proven with two REAL processes against it; (b) no PostGIS work is changed anywhere -- the helper executes no geometry and the jobs' SQL is untouched; (c) 'expected duration' is recorded as the caller's declared estimate, never inferred, because the fleet has no reliable duration predictor and a guessed number written as fact is the defect this program keeps finding; (d) the deploy-traffic lease in _catalog/leases/ is NOT touched or unified with this one -- different resource, different grantor, and unifying them is a decision for the operator, not for this lane.

probe.notApplicable: control lane; graded by a staging contention run (the dispatch's own words). The customer predicate scripts/surface-probe.mjs cannot express this row: no address in any county changes what this lane did. The measured evidence this lane produces instead is two real processes contending for one store, which is stronger than a probe leg here.
